To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the relationship between social capital and life satisfaction is positive and significant; (2) the relationship between the social capital index and life satisfaction is negative and significant; (3) the relationship between trust and life satisfaction is significant; (4) there is no statistically significant relationship between trust and the social capital index.

the nature of social support and the extent to which the relationship between social relationships and well‐being is causal or spurious.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
‘social support’ is a good thing, but that it is not the whole story.
there is a positive association between social support and health, but that this relationship is neither simple nor straightforward.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social support is a useful concept, which has been used in many different ways.
there is a positive relationship between social support (as defined) and health (as measured).
social support is important in the health of individuals, but that it is not the best way to understand the health of populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social support is not a single, unitary construct, and the term is best avoided when discussing the relationship between social networks and health.
social support is a complex phenomenon that is best studied in the context of the social networks in which individuals participate.
the relationship between social capital and health is not a simple linear one.
